prompt.en: A balanced-output tuner is replaced by one with only an unbalanced output. The window line and dipole are unchanged. Which new boundary needs attention?

text.en: The coax-to-tuner input, treating the tuner itself as the start of the balanced system.

feedback.en: The replacement has an unbalanced output. Treating the whole tuner as balanced puts the transition at the wrong boundary.

text.en: The dipole feed point, treating the window-line run as an extension of the unbalanced output.

feedback.en: Window line is balanced. The balance transition needs attention before that run, not after it.

text.en: The new tuner output feeding the existing balanced line.

feedback.en: The replacement creates an unbalanced-to-balanced transition before the window line begins.

text.en: The midpoint of the window line, to equalize losses in its two halves.

feedback.en: Equal cable halves do not define a balance transition. Follow the electrical boundary instead.

explanation.en: A replacement component can create a new interface requirement even if the antenna itself stays unchanged.

prompt.en: A coax jumper will be wound tightly on a ferrite toroid for common-mode control. Which dielectric choice follows the construction guidance?

text.en: Choose foam only because lower loss guarantees better resistance to tight bending.

feedback.en: Low loss and mechanical stability are different properties. Foam does not give that guarantee.

text.en: Prefer solid dielectric to help keep the centre conductor from shifting toward the shield.

feedback.en: Solid dielectric supports the conductor during tight winding, reducing the risk of a short.

text.en: Choose the thinnest insulation because the shield alone keeps the conductor centred.

feedback.en: The dielectric separates and supports the conductors. Thinner insulation is not automatically safer.

text.en: Treat foam and solid dielectric as mechanically identical if both cables have the same Z0.

feedback.en: Equal characteristic impedance does not establish identical mechanical behaviour under tight winding.

explanation.en: Choose cable for its mechanical job as well as attenuation and characteristic impedance.

prompt.en: An older coax jumper passes a low-current continuity check. During a brief transmit test its connector becomes warm and RF readings turn intermittent. Which conclusion fits?

text.en: The continuity pass makes a connector fault unlikely, so the antenna should be investigated first.

feedback.en: A contact can pass a small test current yet heat or become intermittent under load. The connector symptom still warrants direct inspection.

text.en: The result is ordinary cable attenuation, so the connector can stay if total line loss is acceptable.

feedback.en: Ordinary distributed cable loss does not explain intermittent behaviour at a warming connector. A loss budget is not a substitute for checking the contact.

text.en: Retuning at the radio is sufficient if the station-end SWR improves.

feedback.en: An improved match does not establish a sound connector. The local heating and intermittent behaviour still need attention.

text.en: A path exists at low current, but connector contact quality still needs checking before reuse.

feedback.en: Continuity establishes an unbroken path under the test conditions. It does not establish a sound contact under transmit load; inspect and restore or replace the faulty connection.

explanation.en: A low-current continuity test and a transmit-load test answer different questions. Use the connector symptoms to guide the next inspection.
